technical.prompt: What is span of control?
expectedPoints: Number of direct reports per manager

choices.answer: The number of people reporting directly to a manager
distractors: The number of offices a firm controls
The size of a firm's market share

technical.prompt: What are organisational layers?

choices.answer: The levels of management between frontline and CEO
distractors: The floors of a company's building
The steps in a hiring process

technical.prompt: What is the difference between a centralised and decentralised organisation?

choices.answer: Centralised decides at the top; decentralised pushes it down
distractors: Decentralised decides everything at the top
They differ only in office location

technical.prompt: What is a matrix organisation?

choices.answer: Staff reporting along two lines, like product and region
distractors: A company with no reporting lines at all
A firm organised in alphabetical order
A single, strict chain of command

technical.prompt: What is a RACI chart?

choices.answer: Who's responsible, accountable, consulted, informed
distractors: A chart of revenue by each region
A list of the company's awards
A ranking of staff by their pay

technical.prompt: What is a price waterfall?
expectedPoints: Steps from list to pocket price

choices.answer: The steps from list price down to what's actually kept
distractors: A chart of prices rising each year
A fountain in a shop's entrance

technical.prompt: What is pocket price?
expectedPoints: After all discounts and costs to serve

choices.answer: Revenue actually kept after all discounts
distractors: The price printed on the product
The price charged for small items
The price paid in cash only

technical.prompt: What is bundling?

choices.answer: Selling several products together, often at a discount
distractors: Selling products one at a time

technical.prompt: What is good-better-best pricing?
expectedPoints: Three tiers of features and price

choices.answer: Offering three tiers of features at rising prices
distractors: Pricing only for the best customers

technical.prompt: What is the difference between needs-based and demographic segmentation?

choices.answer: Needs groups by wants; demographic by who they are
distractors: Demographic groups customers by their wants
The two always produce identical groups

technical.prompt: What is cost to serve?

choices.answer: Costs of handling, delivering and supporting a client
distractors: The cost of making the product itself

technical.prompt: What is activity-based costing?
expectedPoints: Assigns overhead by activities that drive it

choices.answer: Assigning overhead by the activities that actually drive it
distractors: Charging overhead evenly to every product

technical.prompt: What is SKU rationalisation?

choices.answer: Cutting low-value product variants to reduce complexity

technical.prompt: What is an action title on a slide?

choices.answer: A headline that states the slide's main takeaway
distractors: A title naming the chart type
A heading listing the data source
A title with the client's logo

technical.prompt: What is a storyline in a consulting project?

choices.answer: The logical sequence of key messages behind the deck
distractors: A fictional story told to clients
A timeline of the project's meetings
A list of every slide's charts

technical.prompt: What is overhead allocation?

choices.answer: Spreading shared costs across products or units

technical.prompt: What is price realisation?
expectedPoints: Share of planned price increase achieved

choices.answer: How much of a planned price rise is actually achieved
distractors: The date a price change starts
A price set by a regulator
The price of the cheapest product

technical.prompt: Why should a company analyse profitability by customer?

choices.answer: Some customers lose money once service costs count

technical.prompt: Why do organisations restructure?

choices.answer: To match strategy, cut cost or speed decisions
distractors: Because laws require it every year
To add as many layers as possible
Only to change the company logo

technical.prompt: 200 frontline staff have supervisors with a span of 8. If the span rises to 10, how many supervisor roles are saved, and at $80,000 each what's the saving?

choices.answer: 5 roles, saving about $400,000

technical.prompt: A product lists at $100. Invoice discounts are 10%, year-end rebates 5% of list and freight allowances $3. What is the pocket price?
Segment A has $60 million of revenue and $50 million of cost to serve; segment B $40 million and $25 million. Which is more profitable per dollar?

choices.answer: Segment B, at about 38% versus 17%
distractors: Segment A, since its revenue is larger

technical.prompt: Products sell for $60 and $40 separately. A bundle is priced at $85. What is the bundle discount?
Half of customers buy the $10 tier, 35% the $15 tier and 15% the $25 tier. What is the average price?
expectedPoints: Mix across tiers sets the average price

technical.prompt: $1 million of overhead is allocated by revenue. Customer X is 10% of revenue but 30% of orders. Under activity-based costing by orders, how does its overhead change?
expectedPoints: Customer less profitable than it looked

choices.answer: It rises from $100,000 to $300,000

technical.prompt: In a city of 2 million people, 80% see a dentist twice a year. A dentist sees 10 patients a day for 240 days a year. Roughly how many dentists does the city need?
expectedPoints: Per dentist: 10 x 240 = 2,400 visits a year

choices.answer: About 1,300

technical.prompt: A company announced a 5% price increase but achieved only 3%. What is its price realisation?
What are the risks of widening spans of control too far?

choices.answer: Managers can't coach or oversee their teams properly

technical.prompt: When does a decentralised structure make sense?

choices.answer: When local markets differ and speed matters

technical.prompt: Why do discounts often creep up over time?

choices.answer: Sales teams chase volume without discount controls

technical.prompt: How would you segment customers for a business-to-business software company?

choices.answer: By size, industry, needs and value
distractors: By the colour of their logo

technical.prompt: Why can cutting low-volume SKUs raise profit even if revenue dips?
expectedPoints: Some sales shift to other SKUs

choices.answer: Complexity costs fall more than lost margin
distractors: Revenue and profit always move together
Low-volume SKUs are the most profitable

technical.prompt: How would you turn 40 pages of analysis into a ten-slide executive summary?

choices.answer: Lead with the answer and three key messages
distractors: Shrink every page to fit ten slides
Keep only the charts and drop text

technical.prompt: Why do decoy or anchor tiers work in good-better-best pricing?

choices.answer: A premium anchor makes the middle tier look like good value
distractors: Customers always buy the cheapest tier

technical.prompt: How can a RACI chart fix slow decision-making?

choices.answer: It makes clear who decides and who is only consulted
distractors: It adds more people to every decision

technical.prompt: Why can allocating overhead by revenue mislead managers?
expectedPoints: Overhead driven by activity, not revenue

choices.answer: Overhead follows activity, so complex products look better

technical.prompt: How would you estimate the number of wedding cakes sold in a country each year?
How would you decide which customer segment a client should focus on?

choices.answer: Size, profit, ability to win and competition
distractors: The segment with the most complaints
The segment the CEO likes most
